endorsements.quote: Studies conducted on de‐identified secondary data generally qualify for Exempt or Expedited IRB review, as they represent minimal risk to participants.

The AI system processes real‐world clinical data in ‘shadow mode’—running inference in parallel with standard clinical workflows without producing outputs that enter the medical record or influence clinical decisions.

Stage 2 studies typically qualify for expedited IRB review but require a formal medical device determination: the IRB must assess whether the AI system meets the regulatory definition of a medical device under code of federal regulations and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance, which triggers additional oversight requirements.
Safety stress‐testing with adversarial inputs (e.g., images with severe metal artefact, pathological anatomy outside the training distribution) must be documented prior to Stage 3 application.

Human‐override mechanisms: Technically implemented, frictionless override of any AI recommendation by a qualified clinician—a requirement that must be documented in the IRB protocol and verified in the technical implementation.
Prospective clinical validation: A registered prospective clinical trial demonstrating safety and efficacy in the target clinical context.
Decommissioning plan: Formally documented criteria under which the AI system will be suspended (performance below predefined thresholds, confirmed adverse event, IRB request).

Vendors should provide real‐world performance dashboards including sensitivity, specificity and calibration metrics disaggregated by demographic category and must implement mandatory adverse‐event reporting when misclassification contributes to patient harm or near‐miss events.

Vendors providing AI tools for clinical use must supply written documentation on: data retention schedules; incident response procedures; audit log architecture; and compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule's technical safeguards.
For HIPAA compliance, any AI tool processing PHI must be reviewed by the institutional InfoSec Data Sharing Committee prior to data ingestion (3.3).
validation steps required after any model update before re‐deployment; rollback procedures; and clinician/end‐user notifications when performance shifts are detected.

Fairness monitoring: Beyond individual‐prediction explainability, systematic fairness auditing requires computing performance metrics (precision, recall, F1 score, area under the curve [AUC]) separately for protected demographic subgroups and configuring alert thresholds when performance gaps exceed tolerance.
Configuring on‐premise or hybrid cloud storage with encryption in transit and at rest, role‐based access controls and tamper‐evident audit logging for all data access events.
De‐identification must be achieved at the point of data ingestion, before any analytical use.
Selecting metrics appropriate to the clinical task and reporting them with 95% confidence intervals from bootstrapped test sets.
with clinicians retaining the ‘human‐in‐the‐loop’ role before any autonomous action is executed.
Evaluating the operational fit of AI outputs within existing clinical workflows prior to deployment, including assessment of alert fatigue risk from false‐positive rates.
Article 12 (Record‐keeping): Logs capable of reconstructing system behaviour over an appropriate retention period, including timestamps, model version identifiers and inference inputs.
Article 9 (Risk Management System): A documented risk management system maintained continuously across the AI system's entire operational lifecycle—not as a one‐time pre‐deployment exercise.

Formal AI Act conformity additionally requires a conformity assessment procedure, CE marking and registration in the EU database of high‐risk AI systems—procedural steps requiring regulatory counsel and notified body involvement that must be planned from project inception if clinical deployment is the target outcome.

unlisted_practices: Use product-centric rather than project-centric team topologies for deployment-targeted AI projects so each model has an ongoing operational owner.
Compute and report inter-annotator agreement and set a minimum threshold before model training proceeds.
Do not use unsupervised retraining of clinical AI; require human oversight and validation of retraining.
Redesign informed consent as a transparency statement explaining AI's role, validated performance range, failure modes, and unique risks such as hallucination, bias, and drift.
Apply privacy by design, integrating privacy safeguards from the earliest design stage.
Use federated learning or trusted research environments when multi-institutional data sharing is precluded.
Implement technically enabled explainability (saliency maps, SHAP, LIME) rather than only narrative descriptions.
Stage IRB review to scale oversight with the degree of AI influence on patient care (discovery, silent evaluation, interventional).
Document an Algorithm Change Protocol specifying retraining criteria for adaptive AI systems.
Standardize imaging preprocessing (DICOM LUT, voxel resampling) to support generalizability across vendors.
Assemble multicenter, demographically diverse datasets and address class imbalance to support fairness and generalizability.
